questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What file timestamps cannot show on their own
questions.learningObjective: State what a file timestamp does not establish on its own
questions.stem: A beekeeper's logbook lists the date and time of each hive inspection, and a member asks what the timestamps on those records cannot tell an investigator by themselves.

options.text: They record when a file was touched, but not who touched it or what happened afterwards.
They record who changed the file and when, because the operating system signs every change.
options.misconception: believes the system logs and signs every file change

options.text: They are exact, because a file's clock is read from hardware that cannot drift.
options.misconception: assumes file clocks never drift or change

options.text: They survive deletion, because timestamps are kept in a separate permanent ledger.
options.misconception: claims a separate immutable ledger stores timestamps

questions.explanation: A timestamp is only a clock reading written at a moment, so it carries no identity and no description of the change. Signing every change, perfect hardware clocks and separate ledgers are all behaviours the log gives no evidence for.
questions.hint: A clock reading says when, not who or what.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What timestomping defeats and what survives it
questions.learningObjective: Interpret conflicting timestamps and a later clock correction
questions.stem: A copy of the beekeeper's logbook shows a hive file dated the same minute the beekeeper was logged at a different apiary, and the device's clock was corrected later that same day.

options.text: The file was edited after the clock correction, so its recorded time is now accurate.
options.misconception: assumes a later clock correction fixes earlier recorded times

options.text: The timestamp records only what the clock said when it was written, so it cannot establish order.
The file cannot have been edited, because the system refuses edits during a clock change.
options.misconception: invents a system lock on writes during clock changes

options.text: The two records share a time, so the beekeeper must have visited both hives that minute.
options.misconception: treats a matching timestamp as proof of physical presence

questions.explanation: A stored time is a reading taken from a clock that can be wrong, corrected or set by hand, so it cannot on its own settle the sequence of events. The clock correction only tells you the earlier readings were suspect.
questions.hint: Ask what the stored number actually came from.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a firmware signature in an update protects
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a firmware signature protects against
questions.stem: An update package for a hive-scale temperature monitor carries a vendor signature over the firmware image, and the owner asks what that signature actually buys.

answer.exemplar: A signature lets the device check that the firmware really came from the vendor and was not modified in transit, so a tampered or substituted image is refused before installation. It says nothing about defects, backdoors or exploits inside correctly signed vendor firmware, and it does not protect the data already held on the device once the update is installed.

questions.explanation: Signing binds the image to the vendor's approval, so it stops substitution and in-transit modification. Defects in the vendor's own code and the data on the device afterwards are outside what the signature covers.
questions.hint: Separate origin assurance from content quality.

questions.topic: What an availability-first platform changes about a patch window
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many patch waves fit an availability-first constraint
questions.stem: A fleet of 24 hive-scale monitors runs under an availability-first platform that permits at most 2 devices to be offline for patching at any moment, and every device needs the update.
questions.explanation: With 2 devices patched at a time, 24 devices divide into 12 waves, so 12 rounds of work are required. Treating the offline cap as if all devices could be patched at once would give the wrong answer.
questions.hint: Divide the fleet by the number allowed offline at once.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a memory acquisition gives that a disk acquisition cannot
questions.learningObjective: Identify evidence only a memory acquisition can capture

stimulus.body: Apiary logbook: the controller faulted twice overnight. The log written to the card shows the fault code each time, but the decrypted reading for the second fault is not in any file on the card. The service engineer read that reading from the running console before the unit rebooted.

questions.stem: Which observation in that entry best shows what the memory acquisition added that the disk image could not?

options.text: The on-disk log, because files on the card hold the complete history of the faults.
options.misconception: assumes the on-disk log is a complete record

options.text: The reader's identity, because a memory capture records who was present at the unit.
options.misconception: invents operator identity inside a memory capture

options.text: The decrypted fault reading, because it existed only in volatile memory and never reached the card.
The device serial number, which on this model is stored only in volatile storage.
options.misconception: claims serial data is held only in RAM

questions.explanation: The reading was decrypted and displayed in RAM and never written to storage, so it exists in no file the disk image can contain. A complete on-disk log and operator identity are not what the memory capture contributed here.
questions.hint: Where was that reading actually stored?

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a differential test between two versions is looking for
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a differential test between two versions detects
questions.stem: Stage one: the beekeeper's software counts brood frames, and the vendor ships version 2.4 after 2.3. Stage two: the tester runs both versions over the same recorded input and compares the results.

options.text: Whether version 2.4 runs faster than 2.3 on that same input.
options.misconception: treats a differential test as a performance benchmark

options.text: Whether version 2.3 still works correctly once 2.4 has been installed.
options.misconception: assumes the differential test checks backward compatibility

options.text: Whether the recorded input file is large enough to exercise the parser.
options.misconception: confuses test input size with behavioural difference

options.text: Whether the two versions produce different results from the same input.

questions.explanation: A differential test is a comparison of results on identical inputs, so it locates behaviour that changed between builds. Speed, backward compatibility and input size are separate questions that the comparison does not answer.
questions.hint: What is being compared, and against what?

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A fuzz harness that swallows the crash
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a swallowing fuzz harness distorts its findings
questions.stem: A fuzz harness for a hive-sensor parser runs thousands of random inputs and reports one crash in every three hundred thousand runs, and the owner wonders why that is a poor signal of robustness.

options.text: If the harness catches the fault and carries on, the recorded crash count understates real failures.
Random inputs rarely reach the parser's unusual branches, so the sample is too narrow.
options.misconception: attributes the low count to unreached code paths

options.text: The harness ran too long, and the parser's own state was reset on every run.
options.misconception: blames run length and state reset for the low count

options.text: Three hundred thousand runs is below the number needed before any crash can appear.
options.misconception: invents a minimum run count before crashes occur

questions.explanation: When the fault is caught and the run continues, the harness keeps working while the count stays low, so a clean-looking run can hide real failures. Input coverage, run length and reset behaviour do not explain a hidden crash count.
questions.hint: What happens to a fault the harness catches?

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: An image acquisition that records its digest late
questions.learningObjective: Explain the weakness introduced by hashing after the copy
questions.stem: A technician copies a controller's card to an evidence drive and computes the digest only after the copy has finished, and the owner asks what that ordering weakens.

answer.exemplar: A digest is only meaningful as evidence when it was taken over the bytes as they were acquired. Computing it afterwards over a file that could have been altered, truncated or misread during the transfer means the recorded value cannot confirm what the source actually contained, so the copy's integrity is asserted rather than demonstrated by the evidence itself.

questions.explanation: Hashing after the transfer leaves an unprotected window in which the copied bytes could change unnoticed. The late value therefore describes only the file at hashing time and cannot vouch for the acquisition.
questions.hint: Ask when the recorded value was measured.

questions.hint: Divide the impossible entries by the total and convert to a percentage.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What timestomping defeats and what survives it
questions.learningObjective: Interpret timestamps that collide in a period when the device was off

stimulus.body: Apiary logbook: I checked the card reader's file listing for the hive logs. Three files show the same modification time to the second, and that time falls inside the week the reader sat switched off at the closed apiary. The other timestamps on the card look ordinary.

questions.stem: What does that entry suggest about those three files?

options.text: The three files were copied from another device at exactly the same moment.
options.misconception: jumps to a copy event with no supporting detail

options.text: The reader writes a fixed default modification time whenever it is powered down.
options.misconception: invents a default timestamp behaviour for the device

options.text: The week of closure made the reader reset every timestamp it had stored.
options.misconception: claims a shutdown reset the stored timestamps

options.text: Those times were probably set deliberately, since they collide and sit in a dead period.

questions.explanation: Three identical stamps inside a period when the device could not have written anything is a pattern a deliberate change explains, and uniformity plus an impossible window is the point. Copying, default values and resets are not supported by the entry.
questions.hint: Combine the collision with the dead period.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a firmware signature in an update protects
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a firmware signature fails to protect against
questions.stem: The vendor of the hive monitor signs every firmware update it releases, and the owner asks what that signature does not protect against.

options.text: A compromised vendor build system that produces a correctly signed but harmful image.
An image modified in transit, because the signature would no longer verify on the device.
options.misconception: believes signing leaves transit tampering unprotected

options.text: An older signed image being replayed onto a device that still accepts it.
options.misconception: believes replay of validly signed images is impossible

options.text: A corrupted download, because the signature check would detect the damage.
options.misconception: assumes signing guarantees the file transferred intact

questions.explanation: Signing proves the image matches what the signer approved, so transit modification, corruption and replay all fail or are caught by version rules. A build system that signs a harmful image satisfies every check and still delivers harm.
questions.hint: A signature vouches for bytes, not for intent.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an availability-first platform changes about a patch window
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a patch plan fits its window and downtime cap
questions.stem: A patch notice for the hive monitor fleet reads: 24 units deployed, at most 2 offline at a time, patching starts at 02:00, each unit takes 2 minutes, and the fleet must be fully patched within 30 minutes.

options.text: The fleet can be patched in one pass, because 24 units times 2 minutes is only 48 minutes.
options.misconception: ignores the two-at-a-time cap on parallelism

options.text: The fleet cannot be patched in the window, because the total unit minutes exceed 30.
options.misconception: sums every unit's time instead of allowing parallel work

options.text: The fleet can be patched in the window, because 12 waves of 2 minutes take 24 minutes.
The window is too short for any patching, because 30 minutes cannot cover 24 units.
options.misconception: ignores that units are patched in parallel

questions.explanation: Two devices at a time means 12 waves, and 12 waves of 2 minutes take 24 minutes, which fits inside 30. The total unit time and the single-pass reading both ignore how the work is actually parallelised.
questions.hint: Count waves, not minutes of total work.

questions.stem: A memory acquisition of a hive controller captures 2 GB and a disk image of the same controller captures 16 GB, and no disk content appears in the memory capture. How many gigabytes of captured data exist only in memory?

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a differential test between two versions is looking for
questions.learningObjective: Explain how comparing two builds exposes a defect
questions.stem: A tester asks why comparing the outputs of two builds of the same program on identical inputs can reveal a defect that neither build shows on its own.

answer.exemplar: A differential test compares results rather than intentions, so a build that returns a wrong value and one that returns no value at all become distinguishable even when neither looks obviously wrong alone. By pinning the difference to the change between versions, the test turns an unbounded search through behaviour into a narrow hunt for the specific change that introduced the discrepancy.

questions.explanation: Comparison supplies a reference point that a single build lacks, so disagreement points straight at behaviour that changed. That converts a search across all behaviour into a search across the difference between two known states.
questions.hint: Comparison supplies the missing reference point.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A fuzz harness that swallows the crash
questions.learningObjective: Describe the reporting problem in a harness that catches every fault
questions.stem: What problem does a fuzz harness create when it catches every fault and keeps running without recording anything?

options.text: The target slows down so much that fewer inputs are tested than the plan intended.
options.misconception: blames execution speed for the lost findings

options.text: Faults are swallowed, so the run looks successful and the real failure count is hidden.
The target's state accumulates across inputs, so later results are not independent.
options.misconception: assumes state carryover is the main reporting problem

options.text: Every caught fault is reported separately, so the log becomes unreadable.
options.misconception: invents a flood of reports where the fault is hidden

questions.explanation: Catching the fault and continuing removes the failure from the run's output, so a broken target is reported as a clean run. Speed, accumulated state and report volume are separate issues that the entry does not describe.
questions.hint: What does the run summary end up saying?

questions.topic: An image acquisition that records its digest late
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a late digest can conclude
questions.stem: An evidence sheet records: the source card was imaged at 14:02, the copy completed at 14:40, and the digest was computed and written down at 14:52. What does that sequence allow an examiner to conclude?

options.text: The digest describes the copied file, so it does not by itself show what the source card held.
The digest proves the source card was unchanged between 14:02 and 14:52.
options.misconception: treats a late digest as a statement about the source device

options.text: The digest proves the copy matches the source card, because it was computed from its contents.
options.misconception: assumes a digest over a copy also covers the source

options.text: The 38 minute delay proves the copy was incomplete or was interrupted.
options.misconception: reads processing time as proof of a bad copy

questions.explanation: The value was measured over the copied file at 14:52, so it speaks about that file at that moment and not about the source device. The gap between imaging and hashing leaves the transfer unverified.
questions.hint: Ask which bytes the recorded value covers.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What file timestamps cannot show on their own
questions.learningObjective: Interpret suspiciously uniform modification times

stimulus.body: Apiary logbook: the hive log entries all carry a modification time exactly one second apart, in a perfect sequence, even though I only opened the folder once a week and wrote three files each time. The creation times on the same files look normal and well spaced.

questions.stem: What does that entry suggest about the modification times?

options.text: The reader's clock ran at a different rate during that period.
options.misconception: blames clock drift for evenly spaced stamps

options.text: The folder was sorted by modification time before it was copied across.
options.misconception: invents a sort operation to explain the spacing

options.text: The times were probably written by a tool that set them in sequence rather than by real edits.
The operating system's own indexer edited every file in the folder in turn.
options.misconception: attributes the sequence to an indexer without evidence

questions.explanation: A perfectly regular one-second ladder, contradicting the once-a-week working pattern, is what a tool writing chosen values produces. Drift, sorting and indexer activity would not generate that exact pattern.
questions.hint: Compare the pattern with the described working routine.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What timestomping defeats and what survives it
questions.learningObjective: Explain what evidence survives deliberate timestamp normalisation
questions.stem: An investigator finds that the modification times on a set of hive log files have all been deliberately normalised and asks what can still be relied on.

answer.exemplar: Normalising timestamps defeats any conclusion that depends on the order or the date of the changes, since the files can now be made to look as old or as new as the person chose. What survives is evidence that does not come from the clock: file contents, embedded references, write sequences recorded elsewhere, and structural differences in the data itself that the normalising tool never touched.

questions.explanation: The timestamps are now attacker-controlled, so any reasoning that depends on date or order loses its footing. Content, embedded references and records held elsewhere remain untouched and can still support conclusions.
questions.hint: Ask what the tool did not rewrite.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a firmware signature in an update protects
questions.learningObjective: Judge which update a device should accept on signature grounds
questions.stem: A log shows three update attempts on a hive monitor: attempt 1 carries a valid vendor signature, attempt 2 carries a signature that fails to verify, and attempt 3 carries a signature that verifies but was issued for a different product line.

options.text: Attempt 3 should be accepted, because a valid signature is all the device checks.
options.misconception: ignores that the signature does not match the device

options.text: Attempt 2 should be accepted, because it arrived over the vendor's own channel.
options.misconception: treats the transport channel as the security decision

options.text: Attempt 1 should be refused, because a signature proves nothing at all.
options.misconception: denies that signatures provide any assurance

options.text: Attempt 1 is the only one that both verifies and is meant for this device.

questions.explanation: A signature is only usable if it verifies and if it was issued for the device and product in hand, so only attempt 1 satisfies both conditions. Arrival channel and blanket distrust of signatures both misstate how the check works.
questions.hint: Check both the signature and its intended target.

options.text: The plaintext of data that was decrypted in memory but never written to storage.
The full history of files that were deleted from the card months earlier.
options.misconception: credits memory with retaining long-deleted files

options.text: The firmware image held in the device's write-once memory region.
options.misconception: believes a memory capture reads a separate firmware store

options.text: The device serial number, which this model keeps only in volatile storage.
options.misconception: claims serial data lives only in RAM

questions.learningObjective: Interpret the outcome of a differential run over a corpus
questions.stem: Stage one: the tester collects a corpus of 400 recorded hive telemetry files. Stage two: the tester runs versions 2.3 and 2.4 over the same corpus and records every input where the outputs differ.

options.text: That version 2.4 is correct wherever it disagrees with version 2.3.
options.misconception: assumes the newer build is automatically right

options.text: That the two versions disagree on specific inputs, which narrows where the change lies.
That the newer version introduced a fault on every disagreeing input.
options.misconception: treats any difference as proof of a new fault

options.text: That the recorded corpus is large enough to cover all of the program's behaviour.
options.misconception: reads corpus size as proof of full coverage

questions.explanation: The run produces a list of concrete disagreements, which is a bounded list of behaviour to investigate rather than a general verdict on either build. Neither correctness nor full coverage follows from the disagreement list.
questions.hint: The disagreement list narrows the search; it does not conclude it.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A fuzz harness that swallows the crash
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a caught fault hides a real defect
questions.stem: A member asks how a fuzz harness that catches the fault inside a try block can make a serious defect look like a clean run.

answer.exemplar: When the harness wraps the target call in an exception handler that continues to the next input, the fault is still triggered but nothing escapes to the reporter, so the run ends with a zero crash count and a pass. The defect is real and reproducible, yet the summary hides it, and a pipeline that trusts the summary will release the broken build as if it were sound.

questions.explanation: The fault still fires but is absorbed inside the harness, so the report shows no problem. The result is a pass on a target known to crash, which is worse than no testing because it carries false assurance.
questions.hint: Follow the fault to where the report is produced.

questions.topic: An image acquisition that records its digest late
questions.learningObjective: Compare per-acquisition hashing with hashing after the copy
questions.stem: An examiner compares an acquisition routine that hashes each sector as it is read with one that hashes the finished file afterwards. Which statement best captures the difference in assurance?

options.text: The later hash gives better assurance, because it covers the whole file in one operation.
options.misconception: prefers a single late hash over hashing during acquisition

options.text: Both approaches are identical, because the hash of a file equals the hash of its sectors.
options.misconception: assumes file and sector hashes are interchangeable

options.text: The later hash is weaker only because it takes longer to compute.
options.misconception: reduces the difference to computation time

options.text: Hashing as the data is read ties the value to the bytes taken from the device itself.

questions.explanation: Hashing during acquisition binds the value to what the device actually handed over, so read errors surface at the point they occur. A later hash only describes the file after the fact, when the original bytes are no longer available to compare.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the transfer the hash is taken on.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of an incorrect clock on recorded timestamps
questions.stem: A beekeeper's logbook entry is edited on a laptop whose clock is wrong by a full day, and the owner asks what that does to the timestamp evidence in the entry.

answer.exemplar: The timestamp records the clock's reading at the moment of the write rather than the true time of the event, so a clock error is written straight into the record. If the clock is corrected later, the older entries keep the wrong value and cannot be reconciled automatically, which is why timestamps need corroboration from independent sources such as weather records or other entries.

questions.explanation: A timestamp is copied from the clock, so a wrong clock produces a wrong record and a later correction does not repair old entries. The value must be checked against independent evidence rather than trusted on its own.

options.misconception: trusts a hand-set timestamp to establish ordering

options.text: The true order of the three writes cannot be established from these timestamps alone.
The three files were written at the same moment by one batch job.
options.misconception: infers a single batch write from three distinct values

options.text: File A was the first file written to the card in its entire history.
options.misconception: reads the earliest stamp as the first write ever made

questions.explanation: Once the values are known to be chosen rather than observed, the ordering they imply collapses, and other evidence must supply the sequence. Distinct values do not imply separate moments, and the earliest stamp cannot date the card's history.
questions.hint: The values were chosen, so what do they prove?

options.text: Because the signature covers the bytes as signed, so any defect in them is signed along with them.
Because signatures expire, so they stop meaning anything once the update is a year old.
options.misconception: believes the assurance decays with the age of the update

options.text: Because the signature is stored on the device and can be rewritten by an attacker.

options.text: Because signing covers only the file name and never the firmware bytes themselves.

questions.explanation: Comparison supplies the reference that a single build lacks, so disagreement marks exactly where behaviour moved. That converts a wide search through all behaviour into a focused search over a known difference.
questions.hint: A comparison needs a reference point.

questions.topic: What timestomping defeats and what survives it
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a timestamp is a claim about the clock
questions.stem: An investigator is asked why a file's modification time should be treated as a claim about the clock rather than a fact about the event.

answer.exemplar: A timestamp is written from the clock the device was using at that moment, and whoever controls that clock, or any tool with permission to write metadata, controls the value recorded. questions.explanation: The stored value is copied from a clock that can be wrong or manipulated, so it describes a belief rather than the event itself. Independent corroboration is what turns it into usable evidence.

questions.topic: A fuzz harness that swallows the crash
questions.learningObjective: State what a fuzz harness should do with a fault it triggers
questions.stem: A developer asks what a fuzz harness should do when the target under test faults, and what it loses when it does nothing of the kind.

answer.exemplar: The harness should let the fault escape or record it explicitly as a finding, so the run summary counts it and the failing input can be replayed later. A handler that catches the fault and moves on preserves the run but destroys the signal, producing a clean report on a target that is known to crash, which is the worst possible outcome for a pipeline that gates releases on that report.

questions.explanation: Recording the fault as a finding preserves both the count and the reproducing input, which is what makes a fix possible and verifiable. Swallowing it produces a pass on a target that crashes, and false assurance is more damaging than no result.
questions.hint: The report and the replay case are what matter.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: An image acquisition that records its digest late
questions.learningObjective: Explain the evidence gap created by hashing after acquisition
questions.stem: An examiner is asked why computing a digest only after an image has been copied leaves a gap in the evidence chain.

answer.exemplar: Between the moment the bytes leave the device and the moment they are hashed, the copied file is unprotected: it could be truncated, altered or misread without producing any signal. Hashing as the data is read closes that window by tying the value to the acquisition itself, while a digest computed at the end describes only the file as it happens to sit on the destination drive.

questions.explanation: The late digest cannot detect anything that changed during the unprotected interval, because nothing recorded the copy's state at the time it was made. Hashing during acquisition is what makes the copy verifiable.
questions.hint: Look at the interval between the two events.

questions.topic: An image acquisition that records its digest late
questions.learningObjective: Explain what acquisition-time hashing proves that a later hash cannot
questions.stem: An examiner is asked to explain what a digest computed during acquisition proves that one computed afterwards does not.

answer.exemplar: A digest taken while the bytes are being read ties the value to the acquisition event, so it demonstrates that the copy's contents match what the source handed over. A digest taken later proves only what the file contains at that later moment, and it cannot exclude truncation, misreads or alteration in the interval, because nothing recorded the copy's state when it was made.

questions.explanation: Acquisition-time hashing captures the state of the transfer while it is happening, so the record and the copy are linked. A later hash describes only the current file and leaves the interval between acquisition and hashing unguarded.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two moments closes the gap.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What file timestamps cannot show on their own
questions.learningObjective: Explain how identical timestamps can arise without deliberate alteration
questions.stem: A member notices that two files written seconds apart carry identical modification times, and asks how that can happen without anyone tampering.

answer.exemplar: Many filesystems store modification times with a resolution of one or two seconds, so two writes that fall inside the same tick receive the same value even though they are genuinely seconds apart. The result looks like deliberate manipulation without anyone having touched it, and it means a matching pair of timestamps proves very little about the true order of the writes.

questions.explanation: Timestamp granularity is coarse enough that nearby writes collide, so equal values can be entirely innocent. That means equal timestamps are not evidence of tampering, and they cannot order the writes either.
questions.hint: How precise is the stored clock value?

answer.exemplar: A disk image captures what has been written to storage, including files that survived long after the event, but it misses anything that lived only in RAM: decrypted data, injected code, open connections and content deleted while the machine ran. questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What file timestamps cannot show on their own
questions.learningObjective: State what a file timestamp records and excludes
questions.stem: A new apprentice on the apiary asks the technician to state what a file's timestamp records and what it leaves out.

answer.exemplar: A file's timestamp records the reading of the device clock at the moment the entry was written or last modified, and it says nothing about who made the change, what the change was, whether it was altered later, or whether the clock itself was right at that moment. It is a claim made by the clock about the moment of writing.

questions.explanation: The value is a single reading taken from the device clock at one moment. Identity, content, later alteration and clock accuracy all sit outside what the number can convey.
questions.hint: Think of it as a clock reading and nothing more.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What timestomping defeats and what survives it
questions.learningObjective: Identify the conclusion that deliberate timestamp setting destroys
questions.stem: A tool is run across a folder and sets every modified file's timestamp to a chosen value. Which conclusion does that action destroy?

options.text: The file contents, because the tool rewrites the data as well as the metadata.
options.misconception: assumes the tool alters content along with timestamps

options.text: Any conclusion that depends on the order or the date of the changes.
The filesystem structure, because the directory entries are rebuilt from the new times.
options.misconception: invents a structural rebuild as the tool's effect

options.text: The hashes of the files, because the timestamps are part of the hashed content.
options.misconception: believes timestamps are included in what is hashed

questions.explanation: Choosing the values removes the evidence of when and in what order the changes happened, which is precisely what such a conclusion relies on. Contents, directory structure and file hashes are untouched by a metadata edit.
questions.hint: Think about which conclusion used the times as input.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a firmware signature in an update protects
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the signature check belongs on the device
questions.stem: A technician asks why a firmware signature is checked on the receiving device rather than on the vendor's download page.

answer.exemplar: A page on the internet can be intercepted, mirrored or altered, and a member of staff can be misled about which file is current, so trusting the page proves nothing about the bytes that actually arrive. The device holds the vendor's public key and checks the signature over the image it received, which is the only point where the check binds the installed firmware to the vendor's approval.

questions.explanation: Only the device has the trusted key and the exact bytes it was given, so the check belongs there. A page check confirms what the page said, not what was installed on the controller.
questions.hint: Where are the trusted key and the actual bytes both present?

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an availability-first platform changes about a patch window
questions.learningObjective: Describe the effect of availability-first on fleet patching
questions.stem: Which statement describes the effect of an availability-first platform on fleet patching most accurately?

options.text: It limits how many devices may be offline at once, so patching is planned in waves inside the window.
It removes the patch window, since devices can be patched without any interruption.
options.misconception: believes availability-first eliminates downtime

options.text: It forces all devices to be patched simultaneously so the fleet stays consistent.
options.misconception: invents a simultaneous patching requirement

options.text: It makes patching optional, because the platform tolerates any number of failures.
options.misconception: assumes availability-first removes the need to patch at all

questions.explanation: Availability-first bounds the number of devices out of service simultaneously, which turns one patching job into a series of waves scheduled inside the window. It does not remove the window, demand a single wave, or make patching unnecessary.
questions.hint: What does the policy actually bound?
